notes:
1. Meaning of Socio-Cultural History

  • Socio-cultural history studies long-term changes in:
  • Society.
  • Family.
  • Caste.
  • Religion.
  • Language.
  • Education.
  • Art.
  • Literature.
  • Customs.
  • Institutions.
  • Indian society shows both continuity and change across different historical periods.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indian Socio-Cultural History → Continuity + Adaptation + Change

2. Meaning of Continuity

  • Continuity refers to institutions or practices that persisted for long periods despite political change.
  • Examples include:
  • Village life.
  • Family institutions.
  • Religious traditions.
  • Pilgrimage.
  • Caste identities.
  • Agricultural society.
  • Temple and sacred-centre traditions.

3. Meaning of Change

  • Change occurred through:
  • Migration.
  • Political conquest.
  • New religions.
  • Economic transformation.
  • Urbanisation.
  • Trade.
  • Education.
  • Social reform.
  • Colonialism.
  • Modern law.

4. Sources for Social History

  • Important sources include:
  • Archaeology.
  • Inscriptions.
  • Coins.
  • Religious texts.
  • Secular literature.
  • Foreign travellers.
  • Art.
  • Architecture.
  • Folk traditions.
  • Colonial records.

5. Archaeology

  • Archaeology reveals:
  • Settlement patterns.
  • Food habits.
  • Crafts.
  • Burials.
  • Housing.
  • Trade.
  • Religious practices.

6. Inscriptions

  • Inscriptions provide information on:
  • Land grants.
  • Social groups.
  • Village organisations.
  • Temple administration.
  • Donations.
  • Occupational communities.

7. Literary Sources

  • Important literary traditions include:
  • Vedic literature.
  • Buddhist texts.
  • Jain texts.
  • Sangam literature.
  • Sanskrit literature.
  • Persian chronicles.
  • Bhakti literature.
  • Regional-language works.

8. Foreign Travellers

  • Travellers such as:
  • Megasthenes.
  • Fa-Hien.
  • Xuanzang.
  • Al-Biruni.
  • Ibn Battuta.
  • Marco Polo.
  • provide external observations on Indian society.

9. Indian Society — Long-Term Diversity

  • Indian society developed through interaction among:
  • Different languages.
  • Religious communities.
  • Regional cultures.
  • Tribal societies.
  • Occupational groups.
  • Migrant populations.

10. Unity and Diversity

  • India's cultural unity did not mean uniformity.
  • Common cultural links developed through:
  • Pilgrimage.
  • Epics.
  • Religious traditions.
  • Trade.
  • Political networks.
  • Sanskritic and regional literary traditions.

11. Early Vedic Society

  • Early Vedic society was broadly:
  • Pastoral.
  • Tribal.
  • Kinship-based.
  • Less urban than Harappan society.
  • Cattle were an important measure of wealth.

12. Jana

  • Jana referred to a tribe or people in early Vedic society.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jana → Tribal Community

13. Vis

  • Vis referred broadly to a clan or people forming part of the larger tribal organisation.

14. Family

  • Family was an important basic social unit.
  • Patriarchal tendencies were prominent in Vedic society.

15. Sabha and Samiti

  • Early Vedic texts refer to assemblies called:
  • Sabha.
  • Samiti.
  • They participated in political and social decision-making.
📌 Must-Memorise

Early Vedic Assemblies → Sabha + Samiti

16. Varna System

  • The four-fold varna model developed over time:
  • Brahmana.
  • Kshatriya.
  • Vaishya.
  • Shudra.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Varna → Ideological Four-Fold Model

Jati → Numerous Actual Social Groups

17. Varna vs Jati

  • Varna:
  • Broad theoretical category.
  • Jati:
  • Birth-based social group.
  • Often linked to:
  • Occupation.
  • Marriage.
  • Local identity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Varna ≠ Jati

18. Later Vedic Change

  • Later Vedic society became increasingly:
  • Agricultural.
  • Territorial.
  • Hierarchical.
  • Settled.

19. Rise of Agriculture

  • The expansion of agriculture contributed to:
  • Permanent settlements.
  • Private and family control over resources.
  • Social differentiation.
  • State formation.

20. Iron Technology

  • Wider use of iron helped agricultural expansion in the Ganga valley.
  • Forest clearance increased.

21. Second Urbanisation

  • From around the sixth century BCE, northern India witnessed:
  • Town growth.
  • Trade.
  • Coin use.
  • Craft specialisation.
  • Powerful kingdoms.
📌 Must-Memorise

Second Urbanisation → c. 6th Century BCE

22. Social Background of Buddhism and Jainism

  • Buddhism and Jainism emerged in a period of:
  • Urbanisation.
  • New merchant groups.
  • Political change.
  • Criticism of elaborate ritual practices.

23. Buddhism

  • Buddhism emphasised:
  • Ethical conduct.
  • Middle Path.
  • Compassion.
  • Karma.
  • Liberation from suffering.

24. Jainism

  • Jainism strongly emphasised:
  • Ahimsa.
  • Ascetic discipline.
  • Karma.
  • Liberation.

25. Challenge to Ritual Exclusivity

  • Buddhist and Jain traditions offered paths to religious merit that did not depend exclusively on Vedic sacrifice.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Buddhism/Jainism → Alternative Religious-Ethical Traditions

26. Use of Popular Languages

  • Early Buddhist and Jain traditions used languages accessible to wider populations.
  • Pali and various Prakrits became important.

27. Merchant Patronage

  • Merchants supported:
  • Buddhist monasteries.
  • Jain institutions.
  • Stupas.
  • Cave complexes.

28. Sangha

  • Buddhist monastic community was called Sangha.
  • It included:
  • Bhikkhus.
  • Bhikkhunis.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sangha → Buddhist Monastic Community

29. Women's Religious Participation

  • Buddhist and Jain traditions created formal monastic roles for women.
  • Social opportunities remained shaped by broader patriarchal norms.

30. Mauryan Social Integration

  • Mauryan rule connected large regions through:
  • Roads.
  • Administration.
  • Trade.
  • Imperial communication.
  • This encouraged cultural interaction.

31. Ashoka's Dhamma

  • Ashoka promoted ethical principles such as:
  • Respect for elders.
  • Non-violence.
  • Religious tolerance.
  • Compassion.
  • Welfare.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ashoka's Dhamma → Ethical Governance, Not a New Religion

32. Religious Tolerance under Ashoka

  • Ashokan inscriptions advocated respect for different religious sects.
  • This is an early epigraphic example of state-supported religious coexistence.

33. Post-Mauryan Cultural Interaction

  • After Mauryan decline, India witnessed interaction with:
  • Indo-Greeks.
  • Shakas.
  • Kushanas.
  • Central Asian groups.

34. Cultural Assimilation

  • Foreign-origin ruling groups gradually adopted and patronised Indian:
  • Religions.
  • Languages.
  • Titles.
  • Art forms.
📌 Must-Memorise

Political Migration → Cultural Assimilation

35. Gandhara Art

  • Gandhara art developed through interaction between:
  • Indian Buddhist traditions.
  • Hellenistic and Roman artistic influences.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhara → Greco-Buddhist Artistic Synthesis

36. Mathura Art

  • Mathura developed a distinct indigenous sculptural tradition.
  • It produced:
  • Buddhist.
  • Jain.
  • Brahmanical images.

37. Religious Image Worship

  • Image worship expanded significantly in the early centuries CE.
  • Temples and icons became increasingly central to religious practice.

38. Development of Puranic Hinduism

  • Puranic traditions strengthened devotion to deities such as:
  • Vishnu.
  • Shiva.
  • Devi.

39. Bhakti

  • Bhakti means personal devotion to a deity.
  • It became one of the most influential religious currents in Indian history.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhakti → Personal Devotion

40. Temple-Centred Religion

  • From the early medieval period, temples increasingly became centres of:
  • Worship.
  • Landholding.
  • Education.
  • Arts.
  • Festivals.
  • Local economy.

41. Sanskritisation — Concept

  • Historian and sociological discussions use Sanskritisation for processes by which communities adopt practices associated with socially prestigious groups.
  • It is mainly a modern analytical term, not an ancient historical label.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Sanskritisation → Analytical Concept

42. Sanskrit as Cultural Language

  • Sanskrit became important across regions in:
  • Royal inscriptions.
  • Philosophy.
  • Religious literature.
  • Court poetry.

43. Regional Languages

  • Alongside Sanskrit, regional languages increasingly developed literary traditions.
  • Examples:
  • Tamil.
  • Kannada.
  • Telugu.
  • Marathi.
  • Bengali.
  • Odia.

44. Tamil — Early Classical Tradition

  • Tamil developed one of India's earliest major regional literary traditions.
  • Sangam literature is central to early Tamil cultural history.

45. Bhakti in Tamil Country

  • Tamil Bhakti flourished prominently through:
  • Nayanmars.
  • Alvars.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nayanmars → Shiva

Alvars → Vishnu

46. Nayanmars

  • Nayanmars were Shaiva devotional saints.
  • Tradition recognises 63 Nayanmars.

47. Alvars

  • Alvars were Tamil Vaishnava saints.
  • Tradition recognises 12 Alvars.

48. Tevaram

  • Tevaram hymns are principally associated with:
  • Appar.
  • Sambandar.
  • Sundarar.

49. Nalayira Divya Prabandham

  • It is the major Tamil Vaishnava devotional collection of the Alvars.

50. Bhakti and Vernacularisation

  • Bhakti movements encouraged the use of regional languages for:
  • Hymns.
  • Stories.
  • Religious teaching.
  • Community worship.

51. Bhakti and Social Access

  • Many Bhakti saints challenged excessive ritualism and emphasised devotion.
  • Saints emerged from diverse social backgrounds.
  • Yet caste hierarchy did not disappear.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bhakti Challenged Social Barriers → Did Not Completely Abolish Caste

52. Karaikkal Ammaiyar

  • Karaikkal Ammaiyar was an early Tamil Shaiva woman saint.
  • She is one of the 63 Nayanmars.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Karaikkal Ammaiyar → Woman Nayanmar

53. Andal

  • Andal was the only woman among the twelve Alvars.
  • She composed:
  • Tiruppavai.
  • Nachiyar Tirumoli.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Andal → Tiruppavai

54. Ramanuja

  • Ramanuja was a major Vaishnava philosopher.
  • He developed the philosophy of Vishishtadvaita.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ramanuja → Vishishtadvaita

55. Shankaracharya

  • Adi Shankaracharya is associated with Advaita Vedanta.
  • He emphasised non-dualism.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shankara → Advaita

56. Madhvacharya

  • Madhvacharya developed Dvaita Vedanta.
📌 Must-Memorise

Madhva → Dvaita

57. Vedanta Pairings

  • Shankara → Advaita.
  • Ramanuja → Vishishtadvaita.
  • Madhva → Dvaita.
📌 TNPSC Favourite

Three Vedanta Philosophers → High-Yield Matching

58. Basavanna

  • Basavanna was associated with the Virashaiva/Lingayat movement in Karnataka.
  • He criticised ritual hierarchy and emphasised devotion and work.
📌 Must-Memorise

Basavanna → Lingayat / Virashaiva

59. Vachanas

  • Kannada devotional prose-poems associated with Virashaiva saints are called Vachanas.

60. Akka Mahadevi

  • Akka Mahadevi was an important woman Virashaiva saint-poet.

61. Medieval Islamic Influence

  • From the medieval period, Islamic political and cultural traditions became deeply rooted in India.
  • Important influences included:
  • Persian language.
  • Architecture.
  • New artistic forms.
  • Sufi traditions.
  • New urban centres.

62. Persian as Administrative Language

  • Persian became a major language of administration under:
  • Delhi Sultanate.
  • Mughal Empire.
  • It influenced several Indian languages.

63. Persian–Indian Cultural Interaction

  • It contributed to:
  • Literature.
  • Vocabulary.
  • Music.
  • Architecture.
  • Court culture.

64. Sufism

  • Sufism emphasised:
  • Spiritual devotion.
  • Love of God.
  • Ethical life.
  • Guidance under a spiritual teacher.

65. Silsila

  • A Sufi order or spiritual lineage is called a Silsila.
📌 Must-Memorise

Silsila → Sufi Order

66. Chishti Order

  • Important Chishti saints included:
  • Muinuddin Chishti.
  • Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki.
  • Baba Farid.
  • Nizamuddin Auliya.

67. Muinuddin Chishti

  • Muinuddin Chishti is associated with Ajmer.
📌 Must-Memorise

Muinuddin Chishti → Ajmer

68. Nizamuddin Auliya

  • Nizamuddin Auliya was a famous Chishti saint of Delhi.
  • Amir Khusrau was closely associated with him.

69. Khanqah

  • Khanqah was a Sufi lodge.
  • It served as a centre of:
  • Spiritual teaching.
  • Charity.
  • Hospitality.
📌 Must-Memorise

Khanqah → Sufi Centre

70. Dargah

  • Dargah is the shrine or tomb associated with a Sufi saint.
  • Many dargahs became shared pilgrimage spaces.

71. Bhakti–Sufi Similarities

  • Both often emphasised:
  • Personal devotion.
  • Spiritual experience.
  • Ethical conduct.
  • Criticism of empty ritual.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Bhakti and Sufism → Similarities Exist, But They Remained Distinct Traditions

72. Kabir

  • Kabir criticised religious formalism and sectarian divisions.
  • His verses draw from both Hindu and Islamic cultural vocabularies.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kabir → Nirguna Bhakti

73. Nirguna Bhakti

  • Nirguna Bhakti worships a formless divine reality.
  • Kabir is a major example.

74. Saguna Bhakti

  • Saguna Bhakti centres on devotion to God with attributes or form.
  • Rama and Krishna traditions are major examples.

75. Guru Nanak

  • Guru Nanak founded the Sikh religious tradition.
  • He emphasised:
  • One God.
  • Honest living.
  • Equality.
  • Remembrance of God.
📌 Must-Memorise

Guru Nanak → Founder of Sikhism

76. Sikh Community

  • The Sikh community developed through the teachings of ten Gurus.
  • Guru Gobind Singh later founded the Khalsa in 1699.
📌 Must-Memorise

Khalsa → Guru Gobind Singh → 1699

77. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu

  • Chaitanya promoted intense Krishna devotion in Bengal and eastern India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chaitanya → Krishna Bhakti → Bengal

78. Mirabai

  • Mirabai was a Rajput woman saint-poet devoted to Krishna.
  • Her devotional songs became widely popular.

79. Tulsidas

  • Tulsidas wrote Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi.
  • It made the Rama story accessible to a wider vernacular audience.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ramcharitmanas → Tulsidas → Awadhi

80. Surdas

  • Surdas is associated with Krishna Bhakti and Braj devotional poetry.

81. Namdev

  • Namdev was an important Bhakti saint associated with Maharashtra.
  • His compositions influenced devotional traditions across regions.

82. Tukaram

  • Tukaram was a major Marathi Bhakti saint associated with Vithoba worship at Pandharpur.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tukaram → Vithoba → Pandharpur

83. Varkari Tradition

  • The Varkari tradition centres on pilgrimage to Pandharpur.
  • It includes saints such as:
  • Namdev.
  • Tukaram.
  • Dnyaneshwar.

84. Dnyaneshwar

  • Dnyaneshwar wrote the Dnyaneshwari, a Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dnyaneshwari → Dnyaneshwar

85. Ravidas

  • Ravidas was a Bhakti saint who strongly emphasised equality and devotion.
  • He came from a socially marginalised occupational community.

86. Bhakti and Caste

  • Some Bhakti saints criticised caste discrimination.
  • Bhakti opened devotional spaces to broader social participation.
  • Caste structures nevertheless persisted.

87. Caste — Historical Continuity

  • Caste identities remained influential in:
  • Marriage.
  • Occupation.
  • Social status.
  • Settlement.
  • Ritual practice.

88. Jati Expansion

  • Over time, new jatis developed through:
  • Occupational specialisation.
  • Migration.
  • Tribal incorporation.
  • Regionalisation.
  • Political patronage.

89. Occupational Communities

  • Traditional occupations often became associated with hereditary jatis such as:
  • Weavers.
  • Metalworkers.
  • Potters.
  • Agricultural groups.
  • Traders.

90. Social Mobility

  • Social mobility occurred through:
  • Military service.
  • Landholding.
  • Trade.
  • Royal patronage.
  • Religious leadership.
  • Adoption of prestigious social practices.

91. Tribal–Caste Interaction

  • Many tribal communities interacted with settled agricultural society.
  • Some became integrated into caste-based social structures.
  • Others retained distinct identities.

92. Forest Communities

  • Forest regions contained communities dependent on:
  • Hunting.
  • Gathering.
  • Shifting cultivation.
  • Forest produce.
  • Pastoralism.

93. Peasant Society

  • Agriculture remained the foundation of most Indian society.
  • Peasants supported:
  • State taxation.
  • Temples.
  • Landed elites.
  • Urban markets.

94. Land Grants

  • From the early medieval period, rulers increasingly granted land to:
  • Brahmanas.
  • Temples.
  • Religious institutions.
  • Officials.

95. Effects of Land Grants

  • Land grants encouraged:
  • Agricultural expansion.
  • New settlements.
  • Local elite formation.
  • Temple-centred economies.

96. Brahmadeya

  • Brahmadeya referred to land grants made to Brahmanas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Brahmadeya → Brahmana Land Grant

97. Devadana

  • Devadana referred to land donated to temples or deities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Devadana → Temple Grant

98. Village Institutions

  • Village-level institutions remained important across many periods.
  • In South India important terms included:
  • Ur.
  • Sabha.
  • Nadu.

99. Urbanisation — Change over Time

  • India experienced multiple phases of urban growth:
  • Harappan urbanisation.
  • Ganga valley second urbanisation.
  • Medieval temple and court cities.
  • Colonial port cities.

100. Medieval Urban Centres

  • Urban growth occurred around:
  • Capitals.
  • Forts.
  • Ports.
  • Temples.
  • Markets.
  • Sufi shrines.

101. Temple Towns

  • Examples include:
  • Madurai.
  • Srirangam.
  • Kanchipuram.
  • Varanasi.
  • Puri.

102. Islamic Urban Centres

  • Important centres included:
  • Delhi.
  • Agra.
  • Lahore.
  • Ahmedabad.
  • Hyderabad.

103. Port Towns

  • Examples include:
  • Surat.
  • Calicut.
  • Masulipatnam.
  • Nagapattinam.
  • Cambay.

104. Trade and Cultural Exchange

  • Trade introduced:
  • New communities.
  • New food crops.
  • Languages.
  • Technologies.
  • Artistic influences.

105. Indian Ocean Cultural Interaction

  • Indian Ocean trade connected India with:
  • Arabia.
  • East Africa.
  • Persia.
  • Southeast Asia.
  • China.

106. Arab Settlements on West Coast

  • Arab merchants established long-term commercial and family connections on the Malabar and western coasts.
  • Muslim coastal communities developed through trade and settlement.

107. Moplah / Mappila Community

  • Mappilas of Kerala developed through long interaction between local society and Arab maritime networks.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mappila → Kerala Muslim Maritime Community

108. Christianity in South India

  • Christian communities have an ancient presence in Kerala.
  • Later Portuguese arrival introduced Roman Catholic missions on a larger scale.

109. Portuguese Arrival

  • Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498.
  • This opened a new phase of direct European maritime involvement.
📌 Must-Memorise

1498 → Vasco da Gama → Calicut

110. Printing Press

  • Portuguese missionaries introduced early printing technology into India.
  • Goa became one of the earliest centres of printing in India in the sixteenth century.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Early Printing in India → Portuguese Goa

111. Printing and Cultural Change

  • Printing increased production of:
  • Religious texts.
  • Educational material.
  • Grammars.
  • Dictionaries.

112. European Missionaries and Languages

  • Missionaries studied Indian languages and produced:
  • Grammars.
  • Dictionaries.
  • Translations.

113. Tamil Printing

  • Tamil became one of the earliest Indian languages used in printed Christian literature.
  • Missionary printing contributed to the growth of prose and print culture.

114. Veeramamunivar

  • Constantine Joseph Beschi was known in Tamil as Veeramamunivar.
  • He made important contributions to Tamil literature and grammar.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Veeramamunivar → Beschi → Tamil Scholar

115. Thembavani

  • Veeramamunivar wrote the Tamil Christian epic Thembavani.
📌 Must-Memorise

Thembavani → Veeramamunivar

116. Robert de Nobili

  • Robert de Nobili was a Jesuit missionary associated with Madurai.
  • He adopted aspects of local dress and learning to communicate Christian teachings.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Robert de Nobili → Madurai Mission

117. Ziegenbalg

  • Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg was a Protestant missionary at Tranquebar/Tharangambadi.
  • He arrived in 1706.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ziegenbalg → Tranquebar → 1706

118. Tranquebar Mission

  • The Danish-Halle Mission at Tranquebar became an important centre for:
  • Tamil printing.
  • Translation.
  • Education.

119. Colonial Port Cities

  • European expansion contributed to growth of:
  • Madras.
  • Bombay.
  • Calcutta.
📌 Must-Memorise

Major Presidency Cities → Madras + Bombay + Calcutta

120. Madras

  • Madras developed around Fort St. George from the seventeenth century.
  • It became an important English East India Company centre.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Fort St. George → Madras / Chennai

121. Colonial Urban Change

  • Colonial cities developed new:
  • Administrative quarters.
  • Military cantonments.
  • Ports.
  • Railway connections.
  • Educational institutions.

122. Colonial Economy and Society

  • British rule transformed social and economic life through:
  • New land-revenue systems.
  • Commercial agriculture.
  • Railways.
  • Modern bureaucracy.
  • New educational institutions.

123. Permanent Settlement

  • Permanent Settlement was introduced in Bengal in 1793 under Lord Cornwallis.
  • It strengthened zamindars as revenue intermediaries.
📌 Must-Memorise

Permanent Settlement → 1793 → Cornwallis

124. Ryotwari System

  • Ryotwari settlement assessed revenue directly with cultivators.
  • It became important in Madras and Bombay Presidencies.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Madras Presidency → Ryotwari

125. Thomas Munro

  • Thomas Munro is strongly associated with development and implementation of the Ryotwari system in the Madras Presidency.
📌 Must-Memorise

Thomas Munro → Ryotwari → Madras

126. Mahalwari System

  • Mahalwari settlement assessed revenue with villages or estates in parts of northern and central India.
📌 TNPSC Memory

Permanent → Zamindar

Ryotwari → Ryot

Mahalwari → Village/Mahal

127. New Social Classes under Colonial Rule

  • Colonial economic change contributed to growth of:
  • Educated middle classes.
  • Lawyers.
  • Clerks.
  • Journalists.
  • New commercial groups.
  • Industrial labourers.

128. Western Education

  • Western-style education introduced wider access to:
  • Modern science.
  • Political thought.
  • English literature.
  • European philosophy.

129. English Education Act — 1835 Context

  • English education expanded strongly after colonial policy changes in the 1830s.
  • Macaulay's Minute of 1835 strongly supported English-language higher education.
📌 Must-Memorise

Macaulay's Minute → 1835 → English Education

130. Wood's Despatch

  • Wood's Despatch of 1854 laid out a broad plan for education in British India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Wood's Despatch → 1854 → Education

131. Universities of 1857

  • Universities were established in 1857 at:
  • Calcutta.
  • Bombay.
  • Madras.
📌 Must-Memorise

1857 → Calcutta + Bombay + Madras Universities

132. University of Madras

  • University of Madras was founded in 1857.
  • It became an important centre of higher education in South India.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

University of Madras → 1857

133. Modern Education and Social Change

  • Education contributed to:
  • New professions.
  • Public debate.
  • Journalism.
  • Social reform.
  • Nationalism.

134. Growth of the Press

  • Printing and journalism spread:
  • Political ideas.
  • Reform arguments.
  • Religious debate.
  • National consciousness.

135. Indian-Language Newspapers

  • Regional-language newspapers created new public spheres in:
  • Bengali.
  • Tamil.
  • Marathi.
  • Hindi.
  • Urdu.
  • Other languages.

136. Tamil Print Culture

  • Tamil print culture expanded through:
  • Missionaries.
  • Scholars.
  • Newspapers.
  • Literary associations.
  • Political movements.

137. Education and Caste

  • Modern education created new opportunities, but access remained unequal because of:
  • Caste.
  • Gender.
  • Wealth.
  • Region.

138. Women's Position — Long-Term Change

  • Women's status varied widely by:
  • Period.
  • Region.
  • Caste.
  • Class.
  • Occupation.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Avoid One Single Statement About "Status of Women in Ancient India"

139. Women's Property Rights

  • Different legal traditions recognised forms of women's property such as:
  • Stridhana.
  • Inheritance rights varied across communities and periods.

140. Child Marriage

  • Child marriage became socially entrenched in many communities over time.
  • Nineteenth- and twentieth-century reformers later campaigned against it.

141. Sati

  • Sati existed among some communities and regions.
  • It was never a universal Indian practice.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap
